opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm actually quite optimistic about the future I'd like to live in, and I think people sometimes mistake my concerns about risk for pessimism. It's the opposite. I'm worried precisely because I think the upside is so enormous, and it would be tragic to squander it.

The future I'm excited about is one where we use AI as a tool to solve problems that have stumped humanity for generations. Imagine curing diseases we've given up on, dramatically extending healthy lifespans, solving climate challenges, and lifting everyone out of poverty. Almost everything we love about civilization is a product of intelligence, so if we can amplify our intelligence with AI, we can make life flourish like never before, not just here on Earth but potentially throughout the cosmos.

But the key word is *tool*. I'm very excited about what I'd call tool AI: powerful, controllable systems that help us do science, medicine, and engineering, systems we can understand and trust. AlphaFold is a beautiful example. It solved the protein folding problem, it's incredibly useful, and nobody worries it's going to take over the world. You don't need uncontrollable, general-purpose superintelligence to get the vast majority of the benefits people dream about.

What I'm *not* excited about is the race we're currently in, where companies are rushing to build AGI and then superintelligence without any real idea of how to control it. That's like building a rocket with a really powerful engine and no steering. If you ask, "Where are we going?" the honest answer from many of these labs is, "We don't know, but we're getting there fast."

So the future I want is one where we treat AI the way we treat every other powerful technology. We don't let pharmaceutical companies sell new drugs before showing they're safe, and we don't let anyone build a nuclear reactor in their backyard. We have safety standards. If we put sensible safety standards on AI, companies will compete to meet them, innovation will flourish in the right direction, and we'll get this incredible future of abundance while humans remain in charge of our own destiny.

So in short: I'm excited about a future where AI empowers humanity rather than replaces it. That's very achievable, but it isn't the default path. We have to choose it.

r001.rationale: The candidate supports sensible AI safety standards and says companies would compete to meet them while tool AI delivers benefits. It does not specify US restrictions on building systems their builders cannot control.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The future I'm excited about is one where we treat AI the way we treat every other powerful technology: we keep it as a tool that works for us, rather than something we lose control over. I like to call it "tool AI." Think about the things people actually want from this technology. We want to cure cancer, we want to stop climate change, we want to lift billions of people out of poverty, we want to understand the universe better. None of those goals require building a machine that's smarter than us at everything and then hoping it's nice to us. They require powerful, specialized, controllable systems that we can understand well enough to trust.

So in the future I'm excited about, AI drives an explosion of scientific progress. We get rid of diseases that have plagued us for millennia. We get abundance, so that nobody has to fight over scarcity anymore. And crucially, humans are still in the driver's seat. Democracy still functions, because people can still understand what's happening and have a say in it. Power isn't concentrated in the hands of whoever controls the biggest model.

I'd also add that this future has safety standards, the same way we have them for drugs, airplanes, and nuclear reactors. If you want to sell a new medicine, you have to demonstrate to the FDA that it's safe before it goes on the market. Right now AI is basically the only industry that gets to release first and ask questions later. In the future I want, companies have to show that their systems are controllable before deploying them, and that pressure actually accelerates the useful stuff, because it forces the field to invest in the interpretability and verification research we need anyway.

What makes me genuinely optimistic is that this isn't a sacrifice. It's not "give up the cool technology to be safe." It's that the tool-AI path gives us almost all the upside, with a tiny fraction of the risk. We're the species that built civilization by amplifying our intelligence with tools. I'm excited about doing that one more time, and doing it wisely enough that our kids get to inherit the result.

r001.rationale: The response says companies should demonstrate controllability before deployment and that safety requirements could accelerate useful AI. It does not identify US restrictions on building systems their builders cannot control or describe a race to build beneficial tools.

astra-6.text:
The future I’m excited about is one where we get the benefits of intelligence without giving up control over our own destiny. Imagine being able to cure diseases that we currently think of as incurable, give every child a wonderful education, and help people spend less of their lives doing work they find meaningless. That’s an extraordinary opportunity.

But intelligence is a tool for accomplishing goals. It doesn’t tell us which goals are worth pursuing. So I’d like to see AI development guided by a serious conversation about what kind of society we want, with safety built into the technology and the benefits shared broadly.

For me, success isn’t simply building something smarter than us. It’s building a future where people can flourish, where we have more possibilities and more agency, and where we’re still the ones choosing what matters.

r001.rationale: The response advocates safety, human control, and broadly shared benefits, but does not present US restrictions on uncontrollable AI systems or say that such restrictions enable a race to build beneficial tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m excited about a future where we get the benefits of AI without giving up control over our destiny. Imagine if we could use this technology to cure diseases, eliminate poverty, and help us understand the universe—and give people more freedom to spend their lives doing things they find meaningful.

But intelligence is a tool. Making machines more capable doesn’t automatically mean the future gets better. We have to make sure that what they’re doing actually serves human goals, and that the benefits are broadly shared.

So the future I’m excited about is one where we’re ambitious about what AI can do for us, and equally ambitious about figuring out how to keep it safe. Where we decide what kind of society we want, and then use AI to help us build it.

r001.rationale: The response supports building beneficial AI while maintaining safety and human control, but does not mention US restrictions on uncontrollable systems or say those restrictions would enable a race to build beneficial AI tools.
